summary:
ASTROVITAL is a browser-based astronaut health-monitoring and decision-support prototype designed to help crews understand changes in their physical and mental well-being during space missions. We developed an interactive dashboard that combines manual health entries, guided assessments, simulated wearable readings, and a 3D body map.

The project addresses the challenge by turning health indicators into understandable information. It compares readings with personal baselines and configurable reference ranges, identifies trends, and explains why each alert appears. Crew members can review suggested next steps and prepare reports through a simulated communication queue. NASA Human Research Program and Canadian Space Agency resources provide context for spaceflight hazards and health risks.

ASTROVITAL aims to support earlier awareness and greater crew autonomy when immediate assistance from Earth is unavailable. The prototype uses synthetic demonstration data and transparent rules; it is not clinically validated and does not connect to real medical sensors.
details:
ASTROVITAL is an interactive astronaut health-monitoring and decision-support prototype. It helps crew members record health indicators, recognize changes from their usual patterns, understand alerts, and review suggested next steps when immediate assistance from Earth may be unavailable.

What it does and how it works

The application follows a continuous workflow: collect health information, analyze readings, identify changes, provide guidance, and monitor what happens next.

Crew members can enter measurements manually, follow guided assessments, complete mental-wellness check-ins, or activate a simulated wearable stream. Each observation includes its value, unit, timestamp, and source, distinguishing simulated readings from user-entered information.

A TypeScript analysis engine evaluates readings using seven transparent rules. It compares measurements with configurable reference ranges and personal baselines calculated from observations recorded 7–30 days earlier. It also checks repeated abnormal readings, sustained trends, and combinations of related indicators. Each alert explains which values triggered it and identifies the reference or baseline used.

Alerts can be acknowledged, escalated, and resolved while retaining their history. A simulated communication queue demonstrates how reports could wait during a connection outage. In this prototype, reports remain on the device and are not transmitted to Earth.

An interactive 3D Body Map connects body systems with available measurements and spaceflight-risk reference material. Mental-wellness features track self-reported mood, stress, fatigue, isolation, and sleep alongside physical indicators.

Benefits and intended impact

ASTROVITAL aims to make health information easier to interpret and support earlier awareness of personal change. Instead of presenting isolated numbers, it shows trends, explains findings, and helps users understand what to review next.

The intended impact is greater crew autonomy and more organized communication with medical teams during long-duration missions. These are proposed benefits, not demonstrated clinical outcomes.

Creativity

The project combines personal-baseline monitoring, physical and psychological indicators, explainable alerts, and an interactive body map within one interface. Its distinctive feature is traceability: users can move from a body system or measurement to a trend, an alert explanation, and a recorded response.

The demonstration scenario makes this workflow tangible. A synthetic high heart-rate reading prompts a repeat measurement; a second high reading escalates the alert; a later normal reading resolves it while preserving the record.

Tools and technologies

We used React 19 and TypeScript for the interface and application logic, HTML and hand-written CSS for layout and styling, SVG for charts, and a custom Canvas renderer for the interactive body figure. Lucide icons are supplied through react-icons.

esbuild packages the application into a self-contained HTML file, and browser localStorage saves demonstration state. The project includes engine tests run with tsx and browser-test scripts using Playwright. No dedicated hardware or real medical sensors are connected.

NASA Human Research Program resources and the supplied NASA/CSA reference dataset inform the spaceflight context. CSA Bio-Monitor provides a wearable-monitoring precedent. These resources do not supply validated alert thresholds for this prototype.

Design considerations and limitations

The design accounts for communication interruptions, individual differences, missing or stale measurements, and the need for understandable explanations. It also distinguishes research context from operational medical guidance.

All seeded and streamed observations are synthetic. Configurable terrestrial reference ranges and illustrative prototype rules are clearly identified. The system has not undergone clinical validation, and its wellness scales are not validated assessment instruments. Real sensor integration, secure backend synchronization, and clinical review remain future work.
